question.text: Oral mucocele/ranula: Another human immunodeficiency virus-related salivary gland disease?
question.context: To describe clinical characteristics of oral mucoceles/ranulas, with a focus on human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-related salivary gland diseases. A descriptive and clinical study, with review of patient data. We reviewed 113 referred cases of oral mucocele. The following anatomical sites were identified: lip, tongue, and floor of the mouth (simple ranulas), as well as plunging ranulas. The age and gender data of the patients with oral mucoceles were recorded. The HIV status of the patients and other information were reviewed. There were 30 (26.5%) males and 83 (73.5%) females. Most patients were below 30 years of age, with the peak frequency in the first and second decade. Ranula (simple and plunging) represented 84.1% of the mucocele locations. Mucocele on the lips represented 10.6%. Seventy-two (63.7%) patients were HIV positive; and 97.2% of them had ranulas. Thirty-eight (33.6%) patients presented with plunging ranulas; and 92.1% of them were HIV positive, compared with two patients presenting with plunging ranulas in the HIV-negative group. These results strongly suggest that an HIV-positive patient is statistically (P<0.001) more at risk of presenting with not only a simple, but also a plunging ranula type.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The clinical case strongly suggests a link between HIV and ranulas. The study found a significantly higher prevalence of ranulas (especially plunging ranulas) in HIV-positive patients compared to HIV-negative patients. This correlation is statistically significant (P<0.001).
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The statistically significant (P<0.001) higher prevalence of ranulas, particularly plunging ranulas, in HIV-positive patients compared to HIV-negative patients.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other factors could contribute to ranula formation, the strong association with HIV makes it the most likely answer. Other potential causes of ranulas, such as trauma or congenital abnormalities, are less likely to be so strongly linked to HIV infection.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study shows 72 HIV-positive patients had ranulas (97.2%), and 38 had plunging ranulas (92.1%), with statistically significant higher rates in HIV-positive group (P<0.001). This strong association supports HIV as a risk factor for both simple and plunging ranulas.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: 97.2% of HIV-positive patients had ranulas vs 2 HIV-negative patients with plunging ranulas
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Other salivary gland diseases like sialolithiasis or sialadenitis were not mentioned in the data, but the HIV-specific statistics make this the most relevant finding

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates a statistically significant association (P<0.001) between HIV positivity and the occurrence of both simple and plunging ranulas, with 97.2% of HIV-positive patients presenting with ranulas and 92.1% of plunging ranula cases occurring in HIV-positive individuals. This strongly supports the notion that oral mucoceles/ranulas can be considered an HIV-related salivary gland disease in this context.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: 92.1% of plunging ranula patients were HIV positive, compared with only 2 in the HIV-negative group, with statistical significance (P<0.001).
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other salivary gland diseases like sialadenitis or sialolithiasis were not mentioned as differentials; the study focused on mucocele/ranula prevalence in HIV patients, making it clear that the key differential is HIV status, not other conditions.

olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Seventy-two (63.7%) of the 113 cases were HIV positive, and 92.1% of HIV-positive cases had ranulas, compared to only 2 out of 38 patients with plunging ranulas were HIV negative, indicating a strong link between HIV and ranulas.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other causes of mucoceles (e.g., salivary duct obstruction, trauma, or local tissue inflammation) are well-known, but the data clearly show a much higher prevalence of ranulas in HIV-positive patients, which is not expected from these other causes. The clinical and statistical evidence overwhelmingly point to an HIV-related etiology.
